It's a bit annoying that my favorite is right on the edge of where things started to change. But my absolute favorite is House at Loon Lake. Where a reporter tries to investigate a childhood memory where he stumbled on a house that was abandoned seemingly within a moments notice. Complete with burned toys and areas sealed off with overturned furniture. In retrospect it's tinged with the whole "You guys, I talked to POOR RURAL PEOPLE!!!" theme that would come to haunt it. But it's still one of my favorites. And that's coming from someone who was poor rural people at the time it aired. I think that says something about the tone they strived to reach back then. I mean the only big negative I recall is talking about how the poor rural area was filled with an air of paranoia. And even now I'm more than happy to say that's true for both my home and a lot of similar areas. I love rural america, but we do tend to put visitors under a certain extra scrutiny that anyone would be freaked out by. It was shockingly fair. Not stereotyping one way or the other. No noble savage or stupid redneck narrative.

Notes on camp involved people talking about their memories of summer camp. Again, it's kind of funny in retrospect because it's just about the definition of upper middle class american. But I think that's one of the things I liked about it at first. This American Life presented the reporters american middle class life for both people who were raised in it and outside it. Where later on it was more about an assumption that it was for people within it by people within it. But I think a lot of that is where the charm came from. The reporters recognized some level of absurdity in their situation. These days it's more from a perspective that views anyone outside their background as a subject for a story rather than an audience. Some of their best have gone on to other projects.
